source_text: So, *one* approach I heard about at SF Tech Week (which I liked) was to focus on building a co-op that would help people create other co-ops.  So, the "inner loop" here might be about solving some real-world problems, the "outer loop" would be about enabling that on a technical basis.  The only challenge with this is that, if we come at it from a purely technical perspective, we'd be coming with a solution (outer loop) in search of a problem.  That said, there may well be lots of real-world problems that are amenable to good solutions at the co-op level that are not being developed *because* technology is a barrier, and even with vibe-coding people might not be able to bootstrap those companies, whereas vibe-coding plus an SF stack or a FUTON stack might help lower the energy-threshold that's needed.  Maybe I'm not sufficiently in touch with the normal everyday real-world inner-loop style problems that would be potentiated by this way of working, but it seems plausible that the person I was talking to about this is, and I could help with the technical delivery side.  But it'd be good to know more about the concrete examples (even if hypothetical to start with)

reply_text:
㊥ (gist) This fits what the mission has found. The human problems kept sitting where several parties' preferences meet. A co-op is an institution built for exactly that, because its members are the people on the out-channels. I've added §3.7 (`a7400af`) with six example cases. They're from memory, so an agent is now checking them against real co-ops and looking for more.

㊢ ("concrete examples (even if hypothetical to start with)") The six, each with the old component that won't go away and the place where tech gets in the way:
1. **Couriers own the delivery platform.** This is your DoorDash case seen from the other out-channel. CoopCycle already shares open-source dispatch software among bike-delivery co-ops.
2. **A home-care workers' co-op.** The barrier is Medicaid billing and care-plan paperwork.
3. **Small farms sharing food-safety traceability records.** The old component is a federal record-keeping rule, and no single farm can afford its own system. This one is also a small piece of your Mexico trade scale.
4. **A retiring owner sells to the staff.** The books, the valuation and the governance handover are the hard part.
5. **Gig workers pool their own earnings data** to see what the platform actually pays them.
6. **Freelancers share invoicing and social insurance.** Smart in Belgium is the known example.

Almost all of the tech in these is *collect* and *verify*, the same verbs the client-problem pass turned up.

🈖 ("a solution (outer loop) in search of a problem") I think the co-op framing takes care of that worry, provided the outer loop is built from what several real inner loops need in common, not from what the stack already does. In Arthur's terms, the outer loop is a reusable assembly: member decisions, records, compliance checks and money, handled for several parties at once. Then a new co-op's activation energy goes mostly on its own problem. There are existing outer loops to learn from: Co-op Cloud (shared hosting), Start.coop, the Platform Cooperativism Consortium and Project Equity. The agent is checking what each of them actually provides and where they say tech is the barrier.

🈯 ("the person I was talking to") Who was it, and do you know which inner-loop problems they have in hand? A list from someone who's close to the problems would be better than my table. If you can find their organisation, I could look up what they've already published.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text: (gist) I agree about the order. Understand the topics, see how they hook together, model that, look for ways the model could run differently, and only then build tooling. Most of the SF kernel starts at that last step. I've recorded this in the mission as §3.6 (`18c723f`), with your stack as the worked example.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text:
("inspired by W Brian Arthur") In *The Nature of Technology*, Arthur argues that a technology is a combination of earlier technologies. Each component is itself a technology, so the structure is recursive, and new technologies come mainly from new combinations. Your stack shows both of the diagrams that follow from this:
- **Assembly:** Kinesis → Dell dock → Samsung/DeX → Android → Termux → 4G → zone.
- **Heredity:** the Linux kernel shared by Android and Ubuntu; Kinesis Classic → Advantage2; ssh, mosh and tmux, all older than the phone.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text: (what that suggests for clients) For each client problem, draw both diagrams and ask **which component has persisted longest**. That component is the client's "keyboard". In the §3.4 cases it would be the paper invoice, the 200-page manual, the regulator's rule and the auditor's question. A tool that asks the client to drop that component will probably fail. A tool that builds a new assembly around it, the way your phone-plus-zone setup gave an old keyboard a powerful server, has a better chance. In scattering terms, the long-lived components shape the in-state before any new tool touches it.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text: (open) This also hints at why the economics and data-analysis problems come first. The long-lived components are often institutions rather than devices, such as a tariff schedule or an inspection regime. You can't see those from inside the tech world at all.
